## First-principles sizing

**1. Define the resource constraint (worst-month solar)**

At 35°N in New Mexico high desert, the constraining season is winter — shorter days, lower sun angle, and (controlling for design) you size for the *average* worst month, not a once-a-decade blizzard, since autonomy days absorb short deficits. For a winter-tilt-optimized array (tilt ≈ latitude + 15°, so ~50°, to favor low winter sun angle), this region's clear high-elevation desert air gives one of the better winter solar resources in the US:

- **December/January average: ~4.5 peak sun hours (PSH)/day.** (Summer will be 6.5–7+, irrelevant to sizing since winter is the bottleneck.)

**2. Trace the energy from panel to plug (loss chain)**

Energy from the array to your outlet passes through several lossy stages:

| Stage | Efficiency |
|---|---|
| MPPT charge controller | ~97% |
| LiFePO4 round-trip (charge/discharge) | ~95% |
| Inverter (DC→AC) | ~93% |
| Soiling (desert dust), wiring, mismatch | ~95% |
| **Combined** | **~77%** |

**3. Array sizing**

$$W_p \geq \frac{\text{Daily load (Wh)}}{\text{Worst-month PSH} \times \eta_{total}} = \frac{1500}{4.5 \times 0.77} \approx 430\text{ W}$$

That's the bare minimum. In practice you add margin because: 1.5 kWh/day is a *very* lean estimate (a single DC fridge alone often runs 0.5–1 kWh/day, and anything like Starlink adds 1–2 kWh/day on its own), panels degrade ~0.5–1%/yr, and you want headroom for a cloudy stretch longer than typical. Oversizing the array 1.4–1.8× the bare minimum is standard off-grid practice because panels are cheap relative to batteries.

**→ Recommended array: 600–800 W nameplate** (e.g., 2×400W or 4×200W), tilted steep (~50°) to favor winter output.

**4. Battery sizing (3-day autonomy)**

Battery must supply the *inverter-side* load, not the DC-bus-equivalent, since it's the thing actually storing/discharging energy:

$$1500\text{ Wh} / 0.93\ (\text{inverter}) \approx 1613\text{ Wh/day at the battery}$$

$$\text{Usable energy for 3 days} = 1613 \times 3 \approx 4.8\text{ kWh}$$

LiFePO4 tolerates 80–90% depth-of-discharge without meaningful cycle-life penalty (unlike lead-acid's 50% rule), so:

$$\text{Nameplate capacity} = 4.8 / 0.8\ \text{to}\ 4.8/0.9 \approx 5.3\text{–}6.0\text{ kWh}$$

**→ Recommended battery: 6–10 kWh nameplate LiFePO4** (e.g., a 48V 100–200Ah bank), with the higher end giving margin for load growth and capacity fade over the pack's life (LiFePO4 typically rated to 80% capacity at ~3,000–6,000 cycles).

**5. A constraint first-principles reasoning surfaces that's easy to miss**

LiFePO4 chemistry generally **cannot be charged below 0°C** (most BMS units hard-cutoff charging in freezing temps to avoid lithium plating/permanent damage) and capacity drops noticeably in cold. High-desert NM winter nights routinely go well below freezing. This means either:
- the battery bank needs to live in a conditioned space (inside the cabin, not an unheated shed), or
- you spec a battery with a built-in self-heating pad/BMS (common in quality LiFePO4 units now), or
- effective winter capacity/charge window will be worse than the nameplate math above assumes.

This is worth resolving before purchase — it affects both battery placement and which SKU you buy, more than it affects the kWh number itself.

## Bottom line

| | Bare minimum | Recommended (with practical margin) |
|---|---|---|
| Array | ~430 W | **600–800 W** |
| Battery (LiFePO4, nameplate) | ~5.3–6.0 kWh | **6–10 kWh** |

One flag worth raising: 1.5 kWh/day for 2 people year-round is lean — worth double-checking it actually includes refrigeration, water pumping, and any communications (Starlink/radio), since those are the loads that most commonly get forgotten and would push both numbers up proportionally if added later.
